summary: Weekly PoC check-in focused on TTFT and streaming behavior. Reviewed last week's benchmarks, identified that initial tokens were dominated by request setup and kernel selection overhead. Samir proposed a streaming buffer tweak plus forcing the optimized kernel path for common sequence lengths. Customer to provide longer tail traces; Redwood to provide updated mapping and cost sketch for a short dedicated pilot.
topics: kernel selection and forcing optimized paths
meeting_header: Date: 2027-03-02 | Time: 10:00-10:45 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Samir Rao (Redwood SE), Ava Thompson (RiverMark Head of MLOps), Diego Morales (RiverMark Platform), Priya Singh (RiverMark SRE)
transcript:
00:00 Jordan Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we're on for 45 minutes. quick agenda: run through the latest latency numbers, dig into TTFT and streaming UX, and agree next steps. Samir will walk the benchmark changes.
00:35 Ava Thompson: Thanks Jordan, quick note we had two production incidents last week where the model latency spiked on longer queries, so we're keen to see fixes.
01:05 Samir Rao: cool, so first slide — um I pulled the traces you uploaded last Tuesday. baseline TTFT was about 220ms on hosted with our default kernels, streaming off. Median token latency fine, but 95/99 spikes were dominated by first token, right.
01:40 Diego Morales: when you say TTFT 220ms, is that after auth handshake and connection setup? in our infra we see variable TLS setup times.
02:10 Samir Rao: good question, Diego. our numbers strip out network cold setup if you have persistent connections; the 220ms includes request serialization and kernel selection inside the runtime. so if you're opening fresh connections it can be higher.
03:00 Priya Singh: we do see a lot of short lived connections in staging because our lambda-ish workers spawn per request. that's probably a big factor.
03:30 Jordan Patel: yep that's classic. two levers: persistent streaming connections or a small connection pool, and then runtime level optimizations — which is where Samir will go deeper.
04:05 Samir Rao: right. so item one — streaming. we enabled streaming in the test harness and saw TTFT drop to ~120ms on average because the runtime primes the decode path earlier and avoids waiting for full chunk assembly. caveat: you need to tolerate partial tokens in your client.
04:45 Ava Thompson: partial tokens were okay for chat UI but our downstream scoring pipeline expects full sentences. can you control when to send the first chunk?
05:10 Samir Rao: yes — you can configure the streaming chunk size and the flush threshold. we suggested a 32-token chunk for your workload which balances TTFT and downstream reassembly cost.
06:00 Diego Morales: what about sequence length distribution? our traces have a long tail — 1024 tokens for some analytic queries.
06:30 Samir Rao: important — for very long sequences the KV cache warmup and attention matmul memory can flip kernel choices. our kernel selector currently chooses a fast attention kernel for <=512 sequences and a memory-friendly path for >512. that path has slightly higher TTFT because it loads different kernels and memory configs.
07:10 Maya Chen: also memory pinning can cause page faults if the model is quantized differently. Samir, did you see quantization differences in the traces?
07:40 Samir Rao: yes, we tested int8 quantized weights and a per-channel 4-bit profile. 4-bit had slightly worse first token latency in the cold path due to dequantization overhead on the first blocks, but steady-state token latency was lower.
08:15 Priya Singh: hmm so maybe a hybrid: force int8 for cold start then swap to 4-bit? is that possible?
08:40 Samir Rao: swapping at runtime is expensive. instead we recommend keeping a warmed warmup container with the preferred quant type, or use our fast dequant kernel which reduces the first-block hit. we're going to share that kernel mapping.
09:10 Jordan Patel: can you explain the kernel mapping again in simple terms? we want to know which kernels to force for our common seq lengths.
09:40 Samir Rao: sure. mapping: for seq <=256 use kernel A (fast attention tiled), for 257-512 use kernel B (batched fused matmul), for >512 use kernel C (memory-friendly attention). we can provide a config to force kernel A up to 512 for your pilot if memory headroom exists — that'll reduce TTFT but increase memory usage.
10:20 Diego Morales: do you have heuristics for when forcing is safe? we're tight on G-resident memory on the dev cluster.
10:45 Samir Rao: yes — we look at peak working set on your traces. from your uploaded trace the 99th percentile seq length is 680 but 80% are under 300. so forcing kernel A up to 512 covers most requests and gives big TTFT wins; the long tail will still go to C if we use a hybrid routing rule.
11:20 Ava Thompson: what's the impact on throughput? will forcing A reduce overall throughput by packing less efficiently?
11:45 Samir Rao: slight throughput drop for long batched requests because kernel A is optimized for latency not large-batch throughput. but for your traffic mix — many small requests — we expect better cost per inference because of fewer stalls and faster TTFT.
12:30 Priya Singh: on KV cache, we noticed some misses in the first 2 tokens for multi-turn sessions. is that an ordering problem or cache warm-up?
13:00 Samir Rao: usually warm-up. we found that with streaming and prefix caching enabled the runtime can pre-populate KV frames if you mark the request as continuing a session. make sure your client passes session_id and sequence offsets. also there's a small race if your client opens multiple concurrent streams for the same session, that can evict the cache.
13:45 Diego Morales: our current client creates parallel requests for component scoring so that might be the issue.
14:10 Jordan Patel: suggested change: convert component scoring to a single multiplexed request where possible, or ensure stickiness to a node so the KV cache persists.
14:45 Samir Rao: next, networking: we saw some noise from TLS handshakes in your lambda workloads. persistent streaming cut that out. also enabling HTTP/2 multiplexing helps.
15:20 Ava Thompson: about the TLS numbers — our infra team insists on mTLS and short cert TTL for security, so we can't keep long-lived streams for weeks. any guidance?
15:45 Samir Rao: that's common. you can keep short-lived streams for a session life (e.g., 30s) and still get most TTFT gains. we measured diminishing returns after a few tens of seconds but the first 30s matter.
16:20 Maya Chen: another knob is connection pre-warm: a small sidecar pool that keeps warm connections per app instance and performs TLS handshake proactively. that pattern works well with restricted cert TTLs.
17:00 Diego Morales: let's talk numbers: you mentioned streaming brings TTFT from 220 to ~120ms. can you show distribution?
17:25 Samir Rao: yep. median went from 85ms to 60ms, mean from 220 to 120, 95th from 480 to 260. we have the csv in the benchmark sheet. the long tail is still present at 99th around 900ms due to the >1024 sequences.
18:10 Priya Singh: can we shave the 99th? that's what's hurting SLOs.
18:40 Samir Rao: options: aggressive routing — route long sequences to a dedicated lane with higher memory and pre-warmed model instances; use model truncation for non-critical features; or accept higher cost for that tail with fallback to cheaper smaller models.
19:20 Ava Thompson: cost tradeoffs — curious about dedicated vs hosted for this tail. if we run a small dedicated cluster with memory headroom and pinned kernels, how much would that cost/benefit look like?
19:50 Jordan Patel: we can sketch a 4-week dedicated pilot: two nodes with pinned models, forced kernel A up to 512, hybrid fallback for >512, plus streaming and a connection pre-warm sidecar. that'll show TTFT improvements and tail reduction. Samir will provide math.
20:30 Samir Rao: preliminary: estimated incremental infra cost about 18-22% for your steady queries but reduces 99th latency by ~35-50% for the tail, and reduces error/retry overheads which indirectly reduces overall cost. we'll send a detailed cost sketch.
21:10 Diego Morales: ok thanks. can Redwood run remote simulations against our traces to validate before we spin up nodes? that would help justify internal spend.
21:40 Samir Rao: yes we can run trace replays in our staging runtime with your permission. need the extended traces and a contact for SSO/trace upload.
22:10 Ava Thompson: Diego will upload permissions.
22:30 Jordan Patel: quick note on kernels — Samir will also share a config file that you can apply to your private deployment to force mappings. be cautious about memory.
23:05 Priya Singh: what's the rollback story if forced kernels cause OOMs?
23:25 Samir Rao: automatic health checks. the runtime will detect OOMs and fallback to safe kernel C. we also have a canary rollout for kernel changes that you can use.
24:00 Ethan Cole: any mention of model quantization regressions on scoring quality? our product team worried about subtle hallucinations when using 4-bit.
24:30 Samir Rao: we ran a short evaluation on your eval set: quality delta was <0.5% for most prompts, but a few rare prompts had higher divergence. we recommend doing an eval run on your critical prompt set before switching quant profiles in production.
25:05 Ava Thompson: good. can Redwood automate the eval and alert on divergence?
25:30 Maya Chen: yes — Redwood Optimize can run periodic evals against saved prompts and raise regression alerts tied to a roll-out. we can integrate with your test harness.
26:10 Diego Morales: re: telemetry — what logs/metrics will Redwood need for the pilot?
26:40 Samir Rao: token-level latency, kernel path chosen, memory working set, stream chunk sizes, connection reuse metrics, and a small sampling of raw traces. we'll provide an instrumentation checklist.
27:20 Priya Singh: about privacy — will Redwood need payload data for trace replay? we can't share PII.
27:45 Samir Rao: we can run synthetic or redacted traces if needed. for best fidelity we recommend pseudonymized traces where user IDs and sensitive fields are hashed.
28:10 Jordan Patel: recap so far: streaming + forced kernel mapping up to 512 for most requests, connection pre-warm for lambdas, run remote replay on redacted traces, and cost sketch for a 4-week dedicated pilot.
29:00 Ava Thompson: sounds right. small ask: can you highlight the exact config changes we should make to the client to enable streaming safely?
29:25 Samir Rao: yes — we'll share a snippet: enable streaming=true, set chunk_size=32, send session_id header, enable http2 and keep-alive with max_idle 30s, and backoff on concurrent streams for the same session.
30:10 Diego Morales: one more: kernel forcing — will that require a model restart?
30:35 Samir Rao: yes a restart or a reload; we recommend doing that during a canary with traffic split 5/95. the runtime supports zero-downtime reloads in dedicated mode.
31:00 Priya Singh: okay. timeline: we want to validate streaming TTFT by next Wednesday. Diego will upload traces by Friday.
31:25 Jordan Patel: action items captured. Samir anything else to call out?
31:40 Samir Rao: I'll attach the kernel mapping and an updated benchmark CSV. Also a small script to replay traces locally.
32:00 Ava Thompson: thanks. small nit: earlier you said 95th improved from 480 to 260 — can you annotate which part of the stack improved most?
32:25 Samir Rao: sure — roughly 40% of that 95th improvement came from removing TLS/setup and client-side buffering via streaming; about 35% from forcing kernel path for common lengths; remaining from KV cache pre-population.
33:10 Diego Morales: if we do the dedicated pilot with pinned kernels, will Redwood manage the infra or we do in our VPC?
33:35 Jordan Patel: options: Redwood Dedicated (we manage) or Redwood Private (we provide the control plane and you host). for the short pilot we recommend Redwood Dedicated to iterate faster. we can export configs to run in your VPC later.
34:05 Priya Singh: security review needed for Dedicated. we have a checklist including SOC2 attestation and KMS integration.
34:35 Jordan Patel: we have SOC2 and can do KMS integrations; I'll send the security pack and a short note on KMS HSM options.
35:00 Ethan Cole: any risks to watch?
35:20 Samir Rao: main risk is memory pressure if kernel forcing is too aggressive — mitigated by canary and automated fallback. second is client-side concurrency creating KV cache thrash — mitigated by session stickiness.
36:00 Ava Thompson: ok let's wrap. final recap?
36:20 Jordan Patel: recap: 1) Samir sends kernel mapping, benchmarks, replay script (due 3/3). 2) Diego uploads longer traces and enables SSO for replay (due 3/4). 3) Jordan sends pilot pricing sketch for 4-week dedicated pilot (due 3/5). 4) Priya validates streaming TTFT in staging (due 3/9). We'll meet same time next week to review.
37:05 Priya Singh: thanks all.
37:25 Diego Morales: thanks.
37:40 Samir Rao: thanks folks — I'll follow up with the sheet and config.
37:55 Jordan Patel: meeting adjourned.
